deep.reconstruction:
This page holds no mathematical derivation. It is a page of quotations and bibliographic notes, apparently collected as mottoes or reference material, with a heading at top left read as 'Jdeal' (uncertain).

(1) A Latin passage credited to Euler, Novi Commentarii Academiae Scientiarum Petropolitanae VI, p. 58. Translation: 'Mathematical speculations, if we consider their usefulness, seem reducible to two classes. To the first belong those that bring some notable benefit to common life or to other arts; their value is usually judged by the size of that benefit. The other class contains speculations which, though tied to no notable benefit, are such that they give occasion to advance the bounds of analysis and to sharpen the powers of the mind. Since we are forced to abandon very many speculations from which the greatest usefulness could be expected, solely because analysis is deficient, no less value seems due to those speculations that promise not inconsiderable growth of analysis.' NC VI p. 58 is plausibly the opening of Euler's 'Observationes de comparatione arcuum curvarum irrectificabilium' (E252, on Fagnano-type elliptic-arc comparisons). The identification is from memory and uncertain.

(2) A French maxim credited to Euler, Histoire de l'Académie de Berlin 1748, p. 234: 'There are general truths that our mind is ready to embrace as soon as it recognizes their correctness in some particular cases.' This is Euler's remark on induction in number theory. The precise Euler paper is unsure.

(3) A note on Fermat's theorem a^m ≡ a. The modulus m is tacitly prime; the note writes no mod. One may also compare König's 'Appel au public' with Euler's reply in Hist. Acad. Prusse 1750, p. 530. This is the 1751–52 König–Maupertuis controversy over the disputed Leibniz letter on least action; Euler's 'Exposé concernant l'examen de la lettre de M. de Leibnitz' is E176. The likely reason for noting it under Fermat's theorem is that König's material raised questions about Leibniz's priority or knowledge of number-theoretic results, including Fermat's theorem. That is my inference.

Context: the previous page has Gauss's prime-counting computations and series reversion. The pages fit Gauss's interest in prime distribution and in the inductive discovery of arithmetical truths.
errors: No derivations, so no mathematical errors. The congruence 'a^m ≡ a' omits the modulus; the intended statement is a^p ≡ a (mod p) for prime p (implicit, not an error of substance).

results.what: Statement of Fermat's little theorem a^p ≡ a (mod p), recorded only as a bibliographic pointer to the König/Euler controversy
results.usually_credited_to: Fermat (1640); first published proof Euler (1736); Leibniz had an unpublished proof

results.what: Quotation of Euler on the value of 'useless' speculations that advance analysis
Quotation of Euler on induction from particular cases to general truths
results.modern_name: Euler on mathematical induction/observation in number theory

deep.surprise_reason: The page only copies Euler quotations and a literature reference. Gauss's familiarity with Euler's work and with Fermat's theorem is thoroughly documented (e.g. Disquisitiones Arithmeticae, art. 50). It is of minor interest as evidence of his reading habits and choice of mottoes.

checkable.sympy: all(pow(a, p, p) == a % p for p in primerange(2, 200) for a in range(0, 100))
checkable.asserts: Fermat's little theorem a^p ≡ a (mod p) for primes p (the congruence noted on the page)

checkable.sympy: any(pow(2, 341, 341) == 2 % 341 for _ in [0]) and not isprime(341)
checkable.asserts: The converse fails (341 is a base-2 pseudoprime), so 'a^m ≡ a' requires m prime as an implicit hypothesis

transcription_corrections: In the Latin, the struck letter before 'pretium' is a false start ('p' crossed out), with an insertion mark. The reading 'non minus pretium iis speculationibus' is correct; 'ii' is not a separate inserted word.
'[-et-] unde' — the struck word before 'unde' is a false start; read 'speculationes, unde maxima utilitas...'.
The heading at top left ('Jdeal') is uncertain and may be a different word or a shelf/library note.

Faint pencil 'Hessen'/'Hessen(?)' at top center and the library shelf stamp at bottom ('Cod. Ms. Gauss ... 13.45' or similar) are not in the transcription. The marginal '58' is a folio/page reference.
'Hist: de l'Ac. de Pr.' = Histoire de l'Académie (royale des sciences et belles-lettres) de Prusse [Berlin].
